cells.tense: You are here at the table, and your hands already know the measure.
cells.ask: For a week, in a patch of ground you tend — a pot, a plan, a kid's project — keep what you put in matched to what comes back, with no strain either way.
cells.core:
Where something is growing under your care — a person, a project, a habit you've kept alive — you can take what it gives without a ledger, and give what it needs without measuring. The ones you tend trust the exchange. They know they can take from you in a lean month, because they've watched you take when you needed. That kind of account doesn't need closing.

When something you're tending starts to pay back, don't push it off and don't tally interest. Notice what it hands you — time, ease, a piece of your life — and take it in as plainly as you'd water it. Feed what needs feeding, accept what it grows, and let the exchange sit level through the next few weeks.
cells.sheetLine: The ones you tend can take from you, and be taken from.
cells.verb: give and take finding their level
cells.place: where what is growing is tended

cells.tense: You're bracing for a scarcity that hasn't happened yet, and it's your hands doing it.
cells.act: keep going without checking on anyone else
cells.ask: For one full day, tend something you've planted without tallying what comes back and without asking anyone whether they noticed — hold it steady throughout.
cells.core:
Somewhere in what you hand out, the exchange has stopped flowing. You give more than you have and then watch for how it returns, and that watching tires the thing you're trying to grow. Nobody is keeping score but you. The people near it feel the pull of something owed and step back, and what you're tending grows thin.

Endurance is yours to draw on. Carry something you're growing through a day on your own reserves — no checking whether anyone sees it, no counting what you've put in. Hold it firmly, not with strain. Firm is what lets a thing grow; strain is what tells it that care is expensive, and nobody can afford that for long.

cells.tense: You're still standing where you stopped tending it, as if the next move were owed to you.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Go back to something you were growing and study what it now needs — no repairing yet — then take only the next piece that comes clear.
cells.core:
Something you were tending has gone unattended, and the way back in feels like a debt — as if you owe it a beginning and can't pay. So nothing gets started. The person, or the project, stays exactly where you left it, and you stay at the window, carrying what it would mean to return rather than the small ordinary move returning actually is.

Close attention is what pulls you back. Don't step into the bare place with effort — that isn't how it fills. Instead, go back to something you meant to grow and study it until its need is plain; that study turns the key by itself. Quiet is not the same as absence. What you notice in the hush tends the thing before you ever get there.

cells.tense: You are already balancing the exchange, gently, and you'd say you hadn't done it.
cells.act: write both sides of it on one page and close the page
cells.ask: Before your next talk with someone close, set down what you've given and what you've taken on one sheet, look once, then put the sheet away.
cells.core:
Between you and the people close to you, things stay even because you keep them there — you take less, you give a bit sooner, you say nothing about it. There's a way of caring you run without deciding to. The taking side, the other half, is held too, and the same quiet hand keeps that level. Those close to you have felt the balance hold without ever seeing the decision.

Before you speak about the next thing between you and someone, know both sides first — what you've been handing over and what you've been receiving. Not to fix either. Just to see. What you know sits like a closed page, and what you say after that will land as truth rather than as a correction, and the people who've felt the level hold will finally hear its author.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it even without announcing it, and that's real.

attempts.check: The record's affinity line would license an ask like 'open up to someone', but Nurturing sits in the Spirit house and the seat's own act is tending what's growing, so 'receive' as the Balanced ask may overreach past the signature's Resonance channel; the reader could reasonably say the balance described is about exchange with people, not one capacity being tended. The asks survive being wrong anyway — a half share left on a table, a sprout kept alive, a skill's hardest part repeated — because each teaches something visible the person can run regardless of whether the diagnosis fits. The sentence serving the writer more than them is the Balanced core's closing image of a closed account staying closed; it is the prettiest line in the quartet and the one I would cut first if the reading had to lose weight.
